column4: Punishment descends into the warned people's courtyard and their morning is declared evil; this is the section's dawn raid recast directly as divine punishment reaching the camp.
The messengers order Lot to travel with his family by night because his people's appointed time is الصبح; night movement and an inescapable dawn appointment reproduce the raid's timing exactly.
The destroying cry seizes Lot's people مشرقين, at sunrise, joining the section's first-light assault to the cry heard beside its dust cloud.
The Thamud are seized by the cry مصبحين, as morning begins; both the hour and the sound coincide with the section's attack image.
A settled punishment comes upon Lot's people بكرة, early in the morning, an especially direct instance of punishment arriving like the section's dawn raid.
Iblis is told to raise his voice against people and mobilize بخيلك ورجلك, his cavalry and infantry; noise, horses, and an assaulting force meet in one image as they do in the section.
Prepared cavalry and عدو الله وعدوكم put horses and the enemy-root together as in the section, while their stated purpose is deterrence, marking a moral boundary against predatory aggression.
The divine question أفبعذابنا يستعجلون is the exact haste-for-punishment stance that the section makes answerable by the next morning's arrival.
Lot is told that the last remnant of the people will be cut off مصبحين; the night journey ends in an unavoidable morning destruction just as the raid image requires.
This ayah supplies the destructive action when the command arrives and the town is overturned; 11:81 supplies the appointed dawn, so this row is the actual strike following that announced hour.

The enemy wishes believers to become heedless of weapons and baggage so it can fall on them ميلة واحدة, in one assault; this directly explains the tactical advantage of catching the camp unarmed, while the prayer guard provides the defensive reversal.

Pharaoh's host pursues Moses' people مشرقين, at sunrise; it stages an army overtaking a vulnerable group at the section's hour, but the apparent dawn attackers will be destroyed rather than victorious.

The conspirators swear to attack Salih and his family by night and then deny witnessing it; this is a planned surprise assault on a household and carries the section's explicit moral sense of aggression as injustice.
They plot while Allah counters their plot without their awareness; after the night attack planned in 27:49, the would-be raiders themselves become the unsuspecting side.

The winds فتثير سحابا, stir up a cloud, using the section's ث و ر root for a rising cloud rather than hoof-dust; the rain revives dead earth and explicitly opens onto resurrection, turning the raid-cloud into life and final rising.
One cry is enough and فإذا هم جميع لدينا محضرون: the sound is immediately followed by the whole human gathering before God, combining the section's raised cry, جمع, and last-day culmination.
The granted spoil is property for which the believers urged on neither horses nor camels; it directly reverses the section's mounted raid and its dictionary image of plunder awaiting division.
Pharaoh and his troops pursue across the sea بغيا وعدوا, in oppression and aggression; the chase embodies the section's ع د و sense of an unjust assault and ends in judgment on the attacker.
The promised event comes بغتة, confounds them, and can neither be repelled nor deferred; it states the surprise and absence of reaction-time that make the dawn raid terrifying.
A visitation from the Lord circles the garden وهم نائمون, while its owners sleep; this is the section's vulnerable camp overtaken before waking, with divine judgment as the assailant.

A cloud advancing toward the people's valleys is welcomed as rain but is actually the punishment they sought to hasten; an approaching cloud conceals the blow, as the section's rising dust both reveals and veils the raid.

The fortified people suppose their defenses will protect them, but judgment comes from where they do not reckon and terror enters their hearts; surprise and the failure of refuge enact the section's inescapable assault.
On that day the human being asks أين المفر, where escape is; it states the final-day meaning of the section's charge ending where no avenue of flight remains.
كلا لا وزر answers the flight-question of 75:10 with “no refuge”; its own contribution is the categorical closure of every escape route.
The opponents describe themselves as جميع منتصر, a united host able to prevail; this is precisely the confident human gathering into whose center the section's charge runs.
سيهزم الجمع predicts that the gathered host of 54:44 will be defeated and turn its back, reversing the crowd's confidence at the moment of collision.

People emerge from the split earth سراعا and the ayah calls this a gathering easy for God; their rapid movement into the final حشر carries the section's rushing force and human crowd into resurrection.
A single cry seizes the people وهم يخصمون, in the middle of ordinary disputing; the sudden sound catches an occupied community with no warning, like the camp at first light.
After the cry of 36:49 they cannot make a bequest or return to their families; the ayah specifies the total lack of response-time implicit in the section's unarmed morning victims.
The battle command is bounded by ولا تعتدوا; it names transgression with the section's ع د و root and distinguishes fighting aggressors from the raid's “plain injustice.”
Hatred of a people must not drive believers أن تعتدوا; the ayah directly prevents an enemy relation from turning into the section's morally named aggression.

Repelling evil with what is better can make the one between whom there is عداوة become كأنه ولي حميم; it gives the exact enemy-versus-friend opposition in the section's dictionary definition and then overturns it.
The address لا تتخذوا عدوي وعدوكم أولياء places enemy and allies in the same prohibition, directly realizing the section's definition of عدو as the opposite of ولي.
Allah knows the believers' enemies and is sufficient وليا and نصيرا; enemy and protecting ally occur together, clarifying the relational opposition named in the section.
The rule for dividing war-gain is fixed on the day التقى الجمعان, when the two hosts met; it joins the section's gathered battle-crowd to the post-raid division implicit in نقيعة.

The question about الأنفال is answered by assigning the spoils to Allah and the Messenger and ordering reconciliation; it supplies the moral disposition of gain after the section's raid and before human division.
People surge into one another like waves, then the trumpet is blown and فجمعناهم جمعا; the crowded collision becomes the final gathering that the section says the raid anticipates.
God gathers humanity ليوم الجمع and names that day the Day of Gathering; this is the eschatological destination of the section's physical جمع.
The promised day is يوم مجموع له الناس, a day for which all people are gathered; it states in final-day terms what the horses' entry into a human جمع prefigures.
God sends winds فتثير سحابا, using the section's ث و ر root for a cloud raised and spread across the sky; rain and rejoicing replace the dust and terror of the charge.
The cry seizes the wrongdoers بالحق and leaves them debris; the section's distressed shout becomes here the just destroying sound that overtakes the attacked community.
The people await only صيحة واحدة with no interval of recovery; a single unbroken cry and no respite make explicit the section's sustained sound and sudden seizure.
The day people hear الصيحة بالحق is itself يوم الخروج; the raid's cry is translated directly into the sound that summons the final emergence.
Divine might comes upon a town بياتا أو هم قائلون, by night or while its people rest at midday; an inhabited place is struck precisely when repose leaves it unready.
By morning the garden has become كالصريم; following the seizure during sleep in 68:19, this ayah supplies the black, stripped dawn aftermath that the owners unexpectedly meet.
The cry takes the wrongdoers and by morning they lie motionless in their homes; sound, seizure, and the morning condition form a complete divine raid sequence.
The cry seizes the wrongdoers while Shuayb and the believers are saved, and morning finds the victims fallen in their homes; the selective rescue sharpens the dawn judgment image.
The quake seizes the Thamud and morning finds them collapsed in their dwelling; it is another repeated Quranic formulation of overnight security ending in a ruined morning.
The quake seizes Shuayb's opponents and morning finds them prostrate in their homes, repeating the section's movement from unsuspecting settlement to inescapable dawn aftermath.
Punishment comes to them بغتة وهم لا يشعرون; sudden arrival without perception is the tactical essence of the section's first-light attack.
After the sudden seizure in 26:202 they ask whether they can be given respite; their too-late request states the missing reaction-time in the raid image.
The question أفبعذابنا يستعجلون repeats the section's cited challenge, while 26:202-203 already show that the hastened punishment arrives suddenly and permits no delay.
Those who demand punishment are told it will come بغتة وهم لا يشعرون; the haste motif and surprise strike meet within one ayah.
The question asks what the sinners can hasten if punishment comes بياتا أو نهارا; the uncertain night-or-day arrival makes their demand answerable as an unexpected assault.
The address asks about punishment arriving بغتة أو جهرة and says only the wrongdoing people are destroyed; it joins surprise arrival to the section's moral concern with injustice.
When a town's people sense divine might, إذا هم منها يركضون: they bolt from it; this is the attacked crowd's attempted flight once the inescapable blow is already present.
لا تركضوا orders the fleeing people of 21:12 not to run and to return to their ease and homes; the command closes the escape that their panicked running sought.
When terror overtakes them there is فلا فوت, no escape, and they are seized from a nearby place; proximity and failed flight give the last-day form of a force already inside the camp.
The result of the conspirators' plot is their own total destruction with their people; it completes the reversal begun by the planned night assault in 27:49 and the unseen counterplot in 27:50.

When the two hosts see one another, Moses' companions say إنا لمدركون, “we are overtaken”; this is the exact no-escape instant of an attacking force reaching the gathered fugitives at sunrise in 26:60.
The Thamud rebel and the thunderbolt seizes them وهم ينظرون, while they look on; the blow reaches a conscious crowd too suddenly for defense.
After the seizure of 51:44 they can neither stand nor help themselves; the ayah spells out the helplessness produced by the completed strike.
Plotters are asked whether they feel safe from the earth swallowing them or punishment coming من حيث لا يشعرون; the threat is an assault from an unanticipated direction.
God may seize them in the midst of their movement فما هم بمعجزين; even mobility provides no escape from the unexpected punishment threatened in 16:45.
After every gate of plenty is opened and the people rejoice, they are seized بغتة; apparent ease immediately before capture parallels the sleeping camp's false security.
After hardship is replaced by ease and the people multiply, judgment takes them بغتة وهم لا يشعرون; growth and security hide the moment of attack.
The people are asked whether they feel safe from an enveloping punishment or the Hour coming بغتة; an all-surrounding, unperceived arrival matches the charge that ends in the crowd's center.
The unbelievers remain in doubt until the Hour comes بغتة or the punishment of a barren day arrives; the final event retains the section's sudden, terminal timing.
The warning commands response before punishment comes بغتة while people are unaware; the ayah makes readiness the answer to the section's surprise attack.
They await only the Hour أن تأتيهم بغتة وهم لا يشعرون; the final day is explicitly staged as an unperceived sudden arrival.
The Hour can come بغتة after its signs have already appeared; visible warning still does not yield reaction-time once the event itself attacks.
The Hour is heavy in heavens and earth and لا تأتيكم إلا بغتة; its universal weight and sudden advent articulate the final reality prefigured by the local raid.
The Hour comes بغتة and its deniers immediately bear their burdens in regret; the sudden transition from denial to irreversible reckoning matches the section's preparatory function.
The specified cow is one that does not تثير الأرض, stir the earth; the same ث و ر root and an animal-earth scene reverse the war-horses that actively raise and spread dust.

Moses appoints a known festival day and has the people gathered ضحى, in full forenoon; an announced public confrontation at a gathered crowd is the tactical opposite of a surprise attack at first light.
The Prophet goes out early to station believers deliberately at battle positions; the dawn hour is shared, but vigilance and prepared placement reverse the sleeping, unarmed camp.
Moses answers the overtaken crowd's fear in 26:61 with كلا إن معي ربي سيهدين; divine guidance overturns the apparently closed escape at the end of Pharaoh's sunrise pursuit.
Immediately after the cavalry deterrent of 8:60, the command is to incline to peace if the enemy inclines to it; it fixes the ethical limit separating readiness from aggressive raiding.
Enmity toward a people must not make believers abandon justice; this supplies the ethical reversal of the section's definition of عدوان as manifest wrongdoing.
Retaliation is limited to equivalence and فلا عدوان إلا على الظالمين; the same aggression term is restricted by a boundary of justice rather than licensed as an open raid.
Close companions become enemies on the final day except the God-conscious; the friend-enemy opposition named by the section is reversed at the very judgment its raid anticipates.
People who were enemies have their hearts joined and become brothers; divine reconciliation reverses the section's عدو relation before it can harden into assault.
At Hunayn the believers' great numbers do not help, the wide earth constricts, and they turn their backs; a confident جمع-like force discovers that crowd-size offers neither room nor safety.
On the final day الأصوات are hushed before the Merciful and only a whisper is heard; the vast gathered judgment is sonically opposite to the section's raised, sustained cry.
The section explicitly invokes the dictionary action “raising the voice”; لا ترفعوا أصواتكم sets a moral limit on that same action in the Prophet's presence, against the raid's swelling alarm.
The command واغضض من صوتك lowers the voice, directly reversing the source section's secondary dictionary image of a voice raised and continued without break.
A stone-bearing storm is sent against Lot's people while his family is saved بسحر, before dawn; the same edge of morning separates rescue from the approaching punishment.
The owners go out early على حرد قادرين, intent and confident, yet 68:19-20 show that the garden was already struck while they slept; the would-be dawn actors arrive as the surprised victims.
The misread cloud of 46:24 destroys everything by its Lord's command until only dwellings remain visible; this row contributes the raid-cloud's total, settlement-level aftermath.
People pass the ruins of Lot's community مصبحين; the morning hour that once delivered punishment becomes the recurring hour at which its visible aftermath is encountered.
Lot is ordered to take his family away during a portion of the night; this is the protective night movement that precedes the victims' cutoff by morning in 15:66.

Earlier peoples أثاروا الأرض, worked or stirred the earth, and built powerfully before their wrongdoing destroyed them; the section's dust-raising root here belongs to civilization later judged, rather than to its attackers.
The hostile groups appear جميعا while their hearts are شتى and fight from fortified places; it makes concrete the section's dictionary picture of a gathered yet mixed human crowd awaiting collision.

After battle has subdued the enemy, فشدوا الوثاق commands tightening the captives' bonds; the section's ش د د dictionary sense is the charge upon an enemy, while this Quranic use marks the restrained aftermath of that encounter.
The Prophet's companions are أشداء على الكفار and merciful among themselves; the shared ش د د root relocates the section's forceful charge from a momentary attack to a bounded communal stance.
أمة وسطا uses و س ط for a just or exemplary community rather than physical penetration into a crowd's center; the moral middle contrasts with the raid's spatial midst.
On the final day the crushed mountains become هباء منبثا, dispersed dust; the local dust cloud under hooves expands into the cosmic dust of the event the section says the raid rehearses.
Hell is described as مرصادا, a place lying in wait; it gives the final punishment an ambush structure that corresponds specifically to the section's surprise raid.
After recalling destroyed tyrants, the surah says إن ربك لبالمرصاد; the Lord's watch or ambush position makes hidden judgment answer the attackers who assume the initiative.
The command urges response before a day from God for which there is no refuge; the lack of ملجإ restates the raid scene's closed exits at eschatological scale.
People emerge from the graves سراعا as though racing toward a marker; human beings now perform the headlong rush, but it carries them into judgment rather than into an enemy camp.
The humbled dead emerge from graves like scattered locusts; a dense, disordered multitude replaces the section's mixed camp and prepares the rush toward the caller.
The resurrected hasten toward the caller and call it a difficult day; following the crowd-image of 54:7, this ayah supplies its compelled forward motion and distressed voice.
If the enemy comes من فورهم هذا, in its immediate rush, divine support arrives with marked angels; the ayah answers a sudden charge with equally immediate reinforcement.
The confederate forces come from above and below until eyes swerve and hearts reach throats; attack from enclosing directions gives the camp-level experience of a crowd with no open side.
No prophet may betray entrusted war-gain, and whoever does so brings it on the resurrection day; it carries the section's post-raid plunder into final accountability rather than private taking.
The guilty see the Fire, know they will fall into it, and find no way to turn away; this is the judgment counterpart of realizing too late that the charge has closed escape.
The address says flight will not benefit those fleeing death or killing; it supplies a military formulation of the no-escape claim that the section carries into the final day.

The household privacy rule names the time before dawn prayer as one of undress and repose; it only indirectly supports the section's claim that a first-light target is likely unready, so the connection is contextual rather than an attack scene.
